articles.text: Sophie Roberts began work for the City of Piedmont on October 3 as the new Climate Action Fellow in the City’s Sustainability Division. Roberts is working with the City through Climate Corps AmeriCorps, a national fellowship program that places individuals with local governments and nonprofits to advance sustainability programs. Roberts is paid a stipend by AmeriCorps. She takes over the 11-month post held the past year by Annie Wenslow. Piedmont has a long history of young, active, and bright fellows, now being overseen by Alyssa Dykman. The Climate Corps program requires individuals to serve an average of 40 hours a week. More information on the national program is available at Climatecorps.org. Roberts hails from Connecticut and earned her undergraduate degree in Environmental Studies and Global Studies at UC Santa Barbara. Prior to working in Piedmont, she was a Legal Assistant at the environmental law firm of Lozeau Drury in Oakland. Roberts said that she relishes the opportunity to work in a city where there is a strong sense of community. She is looking forward to working on implementing measures from the City’s Climate Action Plan 2.0, with a focus on increasing the City’s Plan • Contributing to ongoing evaluation and monitoring of the City’s reach codes • Assisting with the design and implementation of the City’s pilot of an electrification rebate program “We are thrilled to have Sophie onboard to work towards our climate action goals and to continue educating the community about ways they can make an impact in this area,” said Dykman Roberts has quickly jumped into her role and is eager to let residents know about the City’s induction cooktop lending program and free compost giveaway program. articles.text: There are limitations on Housing Element input by residents Editor: On October 12, the Piedmont Post published two letters stating that the 6th Cycle Housing Element, or implementation thereof, should be subject to a vote of all residents. It is important that Piedmonters understand the limitations on what a vote can accomplish. Planning for the potential addition of up to 587 housing units is an obligation imposed on Piedmont by state and regional entities. The Housing Element must be adopted by the City Council and certified by the state by May 2023. No vote by Piedmont residents can alter this obligation. California Government Code Sections 65100 et seq. state (as applied by Piedmont) that the City’s general plan, of which the Housing Element is a part, is to be created by the City Council, with specified responsibilities assigned to the Planning Commission and the Housing Advisory Committee. The role of Piedmont residents is to provide input to the process; there is no statutory provision that allows residents to accept or reject a Housing Element approved by the City Council. Furthermore, it is unrealistic to believe that useful resident input to a Housing Element of more than 300 pages could be provided via an election ballot. The letters allege that changes to Zone B (allowing duplexes and multi-family dwellings on City-owned land) would constitute reclassification of that zone, thus would require voter approval. The City states otherIn my opinion, the City has the stronger argument based on a straightforward reading of the cited Code Section. Given certain residents’ hope to delay or derail the Housing Element, I believe that the City Council needs to do a better job of assessing all Piedmonters’ desires and concerns with respect to implementation thereof. Such an assessment could be done via a carefully designed, thorough online survey made available to all adult residents, who would receive notice of the survey by email, on the City’s website, and via postal service. The City Council should publish the results of the survey and, if it does its job correctly, should proceed with implementation in a manner that reflects the survey results to the greatest extent possible. –Dana H. It is important that Piedmonters understand the limitations on what a vote can accomplish. Planning for the potential addition of up to 587 housing units is an obligation imposed on Piedmont by state and regional entities. The Housing Element must be adopted by the City Council and certified by the state by May 2023. No vote by Piedmont residents can alter this obligation. articles.text: Editor: I am writing in support of Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson for two open school board seats. I have had the unique experience of working with both candidates closely during the pandemic as we served as parent club presidents at our three elementary schools. It’s hard to describe what it was like to be in the role of parent club president that year, but we leaned on each other a lot for support, ideas, and to divide tasks that were not typical of parent clubs. We combined forces a lot to find creative ways to raise money for our schools when morale was at an all time low in the community. Both Ruchi and Lindsay were an absolute pleasure to work with. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council Election this year is critically important for the future of our City. Climate Change, the Housing Element, and the City’s Infrastructure needs are certainly at the forefront, and I want a City Council that can best deal with these and other issues in a way that preserves what I love about Piedmont while improving it where needed. I urge you to join me in voting for the 3 candidates I think can best take on these Herculean problems: Betsy Smegal Andersen, Jen Long, and Tom Ramsey. Betsy Smegal Andersen It is rare in Piedmont to think that a single person deserves the most credit for a single accomplishment, but that is surely the case for our soon to be built swimming pool complex. The need for the Council to ride herd on that project to completion by itself compels the re-election of Betsy. But there are so many other reasons to vote for Betsy. With grace and sharp intellect Betsy has tackled every issue the Council has faced. Her roots in Piedmont are deeper than any other person presently on or seeking to join the Council. We are so very lucky that Betsy is willing to stand for another term. Jen Long The City Council made a terrific decision when it appointed Jen to fill the vacancy on the Council. It is indeed noteworthy that the Council chose Jen because she was the only candidate whom all the Council members felt they could support. We the Voters should now ratify that decision. articles.text: Editor: There are many reasons to re-elect Betsy Andersen to the Piedmont City Council – her experience (nothing in city government is simple and she has shown she understands how to develop feasible solutions and implement them), her fiscal responsibility (city budgets are constrained even here in wealthy Piedmont, but Betsy knows how to make our limited resources deliver maximum impact), and her commitment (the number of hours it takes to be up to speed on the council’s agenda every month and to follow up on existing business and to meet with constituents is staggeringly high. pages.text: Wednesday, October 19, 2022 3 LETTERS TO THE EDITOR Continued from page 2 level, with housing units located above. This is good city planning and would save Piedmont taxpayers money. It is common practice for developers to include city improvements in their projects. Why upgrade our aging, outdated Civic Center buildings with Piedmont taxpayer money when we could have new state-of-theart facilities paid for by a developer? –Chris Read Why I am endorsing Andersen, Long Ramsey The Piedmont City Council Election this year is critically important for the future of our City. Climate Change, the Housing Element, and the City’s Infrastructure needs are certainly at the forefront, and I want a City Council that can best deal with these and other issues in a way that preserves what I love about Piedmont while improving it where needed. I urge you to join me in voting for the 3 candidates I think can best take on these Herculean problems: Betsy Smegal Andersen, Jen Long, and Tom Ramsey. Betsy Smegal Andersen It is rare in Piedmont to think that a single person deserves the most credit for a single accomplishment, but that is surely the case for our soon to be built swimming pool complex. The need for the Council to ride herd on that project to completion by itself compels the re-election of Betsy. But there are so many other reasons to vote for Betsy. With grace and sharp intellect Betsy has tackled every issue the Council has faced. Her roots in Piedmont are deeper than any other person presently on or seeking to join the Council. We are so very lucky that Betsy is willing to stand for another term. Jen Long The City Council made a terrific decision when it appointed Jen to fill the vacancy on the Council. It is indeed noteworthy that the Council chose Jen because she was the only candidate whom all the Council members felt they could support. We the Voters should now ratify that decision. In her short tenure Jen has exhibited thoughtful analysis of the issues, a balanced approach to solutions, and a terrific capacity for hard work. A resounding election victory for Jen would demonstrate to the world that the Piedmont of 2022 bears no resemblance to the city that ran its first Black residents out of the community years ago. Tom Ramsey Tom has demonstrated his ability to handle highly sensitive planning issues at a time when the Housing Element is the issue most immediately demanding solutions. As of this writing 14 of the 15 cities in the Bay Area that have submitted their plans to the State have had them rejected. Make no mistake, unless we do this right the State will do it for us. The chance that we will like what the State does to us is ZERO. Tom’s experience as a planner is sorely needed on the Council. His experience on the Planning Commission has demonstrated his ability to balance issues to assure that solutions further the goal of protection of the City that we love. His 7 years on the Planning Commission provide the experience that will guarantee his effectiveness on the Council right from the start. articles.text: Russian-American author Anastasia Edel, a Piedmont resident, will present a 4-week illustrated lecture titled Russia’s War on Ukraine, with classes starting on Thursday, October 20 at 2:30 p.m. The course is being offered by Osher Lifelong Learning Institute at the University of California in Berkeley, where Edel conducted an eight-week illustrated lecture in 2018 on Understanding Russia, a course that intertwines the country’s political and cultural developments with historical perspectives expressed in film, music, and literature. The last four years have proven to be a busy time for Edel. In 2018 she gave the keynote address at OLLI and to the League of Women Voters in Piedmont on The State of US-Russian Relations. One year later she delivered talks at the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco, the University of Washington, and Berkeley City Club Due in part to the publicity generated by op ed pieces she wrote for the New York Times between February and May this year, she was an invited commentators on CNN MSNBC and Bay Area NBC. In the past five years, six of her guest essays an opinion pieces have appeared in the New York Times, with a spike of interest since Russia began its move to wage war on neighboring Ukraine. . Russia: Putin’s Playground, by Anastasai Edel, was published in 2016. Piedmont author and social historian Anastasia Edel, is teaching a four-week course on the Russia vs. Ukraine war at the University of California in Berkeley through Osher Lifelong Learning Institute The course fee for Russia’s War on Ukraine through OLLI is $90 for the four lectures, each of which will be from 2:30 to 4:00 p.m. on consecutive Thursdays, October 20 to November 10. The course will stream live on the scheduled day and time and will also be recorded. Videos will be available on Friday each week. When Russian missiles struck multiple cities across the sovereign nation of Ukraine in February 2020, Russia became an aggressor bent on destroying a neighboring nation with whom it shares centuries of common past. How did it happen? Why does Putin’s regime refuse to call war “war”? What’s behind Ukrainians’ resilience and Russians’ acquiescence? And where does this all end for Russia, Ukraine, and the world? Edel provided some perspective on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine earlier this year with a lecture at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in April. To register for the current course, click on: https://olli.berkeley.edu/programs/courses/russia%E2%80%99s-war-ukraine. Piedmont resident Anastasia Edel is a writer, social historian, and New York Times contributor. She’s the author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, a concise guide to Russian history, politics and culture.

articles.text: The official Piedmont Turkey Trot training is well underway, but it’s not too late to start training for the big race on Thanksgiving morning. Below is the training plan for next week. The full plan is on the race website: piedmontturkeytrot.com. Police officer Nicole Bolden (right) with McGruff, the cartoon dog that “takes a bite out of crime,” cheered on runners as they made the turn onto Vista Avenue, during the 2018 Turkey Trot Turkey hats are the norm Thanksgiving morning 2018 in Piedmont. Most importantly, don’t forget to register for the race. This next week we are building on your fitness and running more than walking. The run/ walk program is a great way to allow your body to adjust to running longer distances and as the weeks progress you should be able to run more comfortably for longer periods of time. You will also add in another day of speed work so head over to Witter Field during non-school hours and run four fast laps. These should feel uncomfortably fast and you shouldn’t be able to say more than 1-2 words if you were running with a friend. A good goal is to try to run the same pace the full lap and not go out too fast in the first 100 meters. Trust me, it’s easier said than done. These workouts help us build our speed and stamina for race day. Consistent work week over week will allow you to feel your best on turkey day. WEEK DAY WORKOUT October 24 Monday Run 3 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Wednesday 5 min jog warm up 4x 1 lap around Witter track, 2 min break between laps 5 min jog cool down Saturday Run 4 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x
articles.title: How to train for Piedmont Turkey Trot

articles.text: Join Fire Chief Brannigan for citywide drill on November 5 Many Piedmonters vividly remember the 1991 Tunnel Fire in the Oakland hills, which killed 25 people and destroyed more than 2,500 homes. While Piedmont escaped the devastation 26 years ago the threat is more present now because of climate change, which has made wildfires more frequent and destructive. As your Fire Chief, I strive daily to ensure our City government is poised to protect this community in a disaster. In an emergency, the best efforts of public agencies alone will not be enough. Our community needs to be ready for wildfire, and can do so with three simple steps. 1. First, make first responders can reach you in a disaster. If you aren’t yet registered for AC Alert emergency notifications, sign up now. Piedmont and Alameda County public safety officials will use AC Alert to send evacuation warnings and orders in a fire, earthquake, or other emergency. Visit acalert.org or text your zip code to 888777 to register. Bookmark community.zonehaven.com on your computer and phone. In a wildfire, emergency responders will use this site to post real-time, location-specific evacuation instructions and updates. 2. Everyone should do pack or refresh a “go-bag.” In a wildfire, you could have only moments to leave. Everyone in your household should have a go-bag ready with the items they’ll need if they had to evacuate, like a map, cash, and a paper list of phone numbers for essential contacts. Make sure your go-bag is light enough to carry in case you need to leave your vehicle and evacuate on foot – a real possibility in a disaster. 3. Finally, think about what routes you would use to evacuate in a fire. Identify two routes away from your home by car and two by foot. Mark them on the map you keep in your go-bag. For driving routes, focus on main roads that connect with major streets and highways. Bigger roads with more capacity are less likely to get blocked during an evacuation. Everyone should be encouraged to review and practice your evacuation routes with your household, carrying your go-bags with you. Regular practice ensures everyone will know what to do in an emergency, when you must act quickly. Wildfire Evacuation Drill in Piedmont The City of Piedmont will hold its first-ever wildfire evacuation drill on Saturday, November 5. Residents in the Maxwelton neighborhood above Moraga will practice evacuating their homes, while the rest of the City is invited to participate with an at-home preparedness activity. Afterwards, come to the Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, at 10 a.m. for a debriefing where you’ll have the opportunity to share observations from your experience, ask questions, and speak directly with emergency responders. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/wildfiredrill to learn more and sign up to participate. Share this link with your friends, family, and neighbors. The more we all take steps to prepare, the stronger and more resilient our community will be in a disaster. I look forward to seeing you on November 5th.
articles.title: Take 3 steps today to prepare for a wildfire

articles.text: On November 8 Piedmont voters will elect three individuals for the City Council, and two people for the School Board. In addition to local elections, the November 8 ballot includes candidates for U.S. Senate, Congress, statewide elected offices, County officials, and seven statewide ballot measures. Voter registration deadline: October 24 The last day to register to vote for the November 8 election is Monday, October 24. Those already registered are encouraged to check their registration status online at Voterstatus.sos.ca.gov before October 24 to confirm that the information is correct. Residents will need to re-register if they have moved, changed their name, or wish to change their political party preference. Voter registration forms are available at the City Clerk’s Office at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue, and from the Registrar of Voters at Acvote.org/voting/register-to-vote. You can also register to vote online at Registertovote.ca.gov. Ways to Vote All registered voters will receive a vote-by-mail ballot for the November 8 election. Ballots were mailed starting Monday, October 10. Voters can turn in their ballots by mail or at the official Registrar of Voters drop box at the corner of Highland Avenue and Highland Way. • Voting by Mail Ballots mailed through the post office must be postmarked by November 8th. • Ballot Drop Boxes Ballots can be turned in 24 hours a day at any of the 66 official Registrar of Voters secure ballot drop boxes across Alameda County. In Piedmont, there is a ballot drop box located near the mailboxes at Highland Way and Mountain Avenue. The Registrar of Voters picks up ballots from the drop boxes every day. The last pickup will be 8:00 p.m. on Tuesday, November 8th. Postage is not required for ballots submitted at the drop box. • Voting in Person Polling booths will be open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. from Saturday through Monday, November 5-7. And from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on election day, Tuesday, November 8. Voting in Piedmont will take place at the Veterans Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue. Sample Ballot & Voter Information Pamphlet The Registrar of Voters began mailing Sample Ballot and Voter Information pamphlets to registered voters on September 29. Any voter who did not receive a sample ballot or who has questions should contact the Alameda County Registrar of Voters Office at 272-6933 or Acvote. org/index.
articles.title: November 8 General Election Information

articles.text: The Alameda County Registrar of Voters is seeking poll workers for the November 8, 2022 election. Poll workers play a critical role in making voting accessible to all community members – and get paid to do it. Workers are needed throughout Alameda County from Saturday, November 5 through Tuesday, November 8, election day. Interested community members can sign up online to volunteer at acgov.org/rovform_app/ewapply. The application is simple and takes just a few minutes to complete. Job details Poll workers are paid volunteers who perform tasks including: • Setting up and closing a polling place • Helping voters understand their rights • Protecting ballots and voting equipment The County Registrar of Voters office provides training for poll workers. Individuals are paid for training and time served as a poll worker. No special skills are required to be a poll worker. Eligibility requirements: • Must be a registered voter in California • Must be a legal permanent resident or green card holder • An eligible high school student Bilingual Poll Workers Sought Bilingual poll workers are especially needed. In Alameda County, assistance is provided to voters in Burmese, Chinese, Hindi, Khmer, Korean, Laotian, Mien, Mongolian, Punjabi, Spanish, Tagalog, Telugu, and Vietnamese. Residents fluent in any of these languages are urged to consider volunteering. Interested residents can find more information about volunteering as a poll worker at acvote.org/community/become-anelection-worker or by calling the Alameda County Registrar of Voters office at 510-272-6973.
articles.title: Poll workers needed for Nov. 8 Election

articles.text: Joshua Muller joined the city staff on September 6 as an Assistant Planner. Muller, 26, received a Bachelor’s degree in Landscape Architecture and a Master’s degree in City Planning, both from Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo. A native of San Francisco, he graduated from Lowell High, and most recently was in the Planning Department with the city of Lafayette. He takes over a role in Piedmont previously held by Planning Technician Suzanne Hartman. His job will primarily involve reviewing applications for remodels and new construction in Piedmont. “There are multiple thresholds for whether a project needs design review, to make sure it conforms to the city’s design guidelines and zoning code and general planning guidelines. I review those projects that are submitted to determine whether they’re complete or incomplete,” explained Muller. The Planning and Building Department office is located at City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. Newly hired Assistant Planner Joshua Muller.
articles.title: Joshua Muller joins city staff as Asst. Planner

Police officer Nicole Bolden (right) with McGruff, the cartoon dog that “takes a bite out of crime,” cheered on runners as they made the turn onto Vista Avenue, during the 2018 Turkey Trot Turkey hats are the norm Thanksgiving morning 2018 in Piedmont. Most importantly, don’t forget to register for the race. This next week we are building on your fitness and running more than walking. articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) has released a video identifying the underlying causes of California’s constant public school funding battles. A short film explains explains how the 1978 passage of Proposition 13 resulted in California having one of the country’s lowest public school funding levels, and why this structural deficit creates a constant struggle for public school funding. The video can be viewed at www.piedmontedfoundation.org. The thoughtful, polished film has all the hallmarks of a highcost presentation from a professional marketing company but was nearly free for PEF. The Palo Alto School Unified District’s Partners in Education foundation created the original video. They then open-sourced it, allowing any California education foundation to customize and use it for a very minimal cost. “Palo Alto is so invested in helping to strengthen the Bay Area’s educational foundations,” says PEF director Heather Frank. “Not only was their idea brilliant, but it also allowed us to develop an educational video for the Giving Campaign that we wouldn’t have been able to afford otherwise. That support is so helpful.” The Giving Campaign is PEF’s largest annual fundraiser, a yearly effort that helps the Piedmont Unified School District combat the gaps created by California’s chronic underfunding of public schools. This year’s campaign aims to raise $3.5 million for Piedmont’s students. Piedmont is not alone in the need for public school fundraising. Because of California’s ongoing school funding crisis, many public school districts have formed their own education foundations similar to PEF. Their misData on state-by-state school funding levels.

Foundation debuts educational video Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) has released a video identifying the underlying causes of California’s constant public school funding battles. A short film explains explains how the 1978 passage of Proposition 13 resulted in California having one of the country’s lowest public school funding levels, and why this structural deficit creates a constant struggle for public school funding. The video can be viewed at www.piedmontedfoundation.org. The thoughtful, polished film has all the hallmarks of a highcost presentation from a professional marketing company but was nearly free for PEF. The Palo Alto School Unified District’s Partners in Education foundation created the original video. They then open-sourced it, allowing any California education foundation to customize and use it for a very minimal cost. “Palo Alto is so invested in helping to strengthen the Bay Area’s educational foundations,” says PEF director Heather Frank. “Not only was their idea brilliant, but it also allowed us to develop an educational video for the Giving Campaign that we wouldn’t have been able to afford otherwise. That support is so helpful.” The Giving Campaign is PEF’s largest annual fundraiser, a yearly effort that helps the Piedmont Unified School District combat the gaps created by California’s chronic underfunding of public schools. This year’s campaign aims to raise $3.5 million for Piedmont’s students. Piedmont is not alone in the need for public school fundraising. Because of California’s ongoing school funding crisis, many public school districts have formed their own education foundations similar to PEF. Their misPhotos by Katie Sharafi PMS students supporting the Giving Campaign: Sai Ahuja (left), Lettie Moore, Violet Snyder, and Ellia Sharafi. Data on state-by-state school funding levels. The best quality in all departments Serving our community for 120 years CURRENT STORE HOURS Monday through Saturday – 9:00 am to 8:00 pm Sunday – 9:00 am to 7:00 pm Piedmont Avenue • Oakland, California 94611 • 510-653-8181 Open Seven Days • Free Parking PMS students walking to school: Ben Gitter (left), Rory Hull, and Spencer Lee Tsai. sion is to provide the economic support required to give students a high-quality education beyond the bare-bones elements funded by the state. PEF is part of a group of such organizations, the Bay Area Education Foundations (BAEF) consortium. The 36-member group collaborates in numerous ways, from annual round table discussions to facilitating communication among members to address questions and share policies. Upcoming topics include teacher retention and declining enrollment, both state-wide issues. “It’s a lovely collaboration between all the foundations,” says Giving Campaign co-chair Katie Sharafi. “And a great example of that is the Palo Alto foundation sharing their work with other districts.” PEF also contributes to the consortium, sharing policy and contract structures and its experience on more cutting-edge issues, such as school support organization fiscal sponsorships. “Because we’ve done the work on many things, we can share and help strengthen other education foundations,” says Frank. PEF’s primary purpose continues to be its critical fundraising work for Piedmont schools. “Raising this much money every year is a huge endeavor, and public school districts don’t have the personnel and expertise to put on major fundraising campaigns,” explains Frank. “And because the foundation is separate from the school district, PEF can reflect community priorities when deciding how to distribute funds.” And as the video makes clear, public schools throughout California will continue to contend with funding challenges until the issues underlying the deficits are rectified. “Piedmont is not alone in this fundraising experience,” says Giving Campaign co-chair Sharafi. “All California’s public school districts are trying to find creative ways to fill their funding gaps.” To learn more about the Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign or to donate, please visit www.piedmontedfoundation.org.

articles.text: Last summer a cohort of Chabot’s Galaxy Explorer high school students worked at NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley as part of a larger partnership between NASA Ames and Chabot Space & Science Center in Oakland. The full-time internships placed each student in a department for project work and close mentorship by NASA staff. Students were paired with scientists and staff based on their interests and future career paths. For Piedmont High senior Sage Mosley, a 3-year Galaxy Explorer, the passion for space began at a young age. She began exploring the cosmos at age nine with a Planet Project and continued to Space Camp during middle school for two summers at the U.S. Space and Rocket Center in Alabama. She has been an intern at Chabot Space & Science Center since her freshman year in high school. “In 3rd grade, I told my parents I wanted to work for NASA,” said Mosley. “Eight years later, I was reading my offer letter to intern at Ames Research Center. I started jumping up and down, and I immediately ran to share the news. My family and friends were beyond proud.” Mosley plans to study Aerospace Engineering after graduation, and ultimately her goal is to become a NASA astronaut. “The most exciting thing about the internship is meeting people with the same passions as mine. While I was nervous to be the youngest in the room on my first day, I was welcomed into a super friendly environment at Ames. Through my example, I hope to encourage others my age to follow their dreams and keep going until they succeed.” Mosley is one of eight Galaxy Explorers who interned at NASA Ames this summer. The interns learned directly from mentors in the field, working on projects in supercomputing, data analytics, rotorcraft aeromechanics, lunar missions, public engagement, computer science and STEM engagement. Megan Hiller is an intern at Chabot Space & Science Center, located at 10000 Skyline Blvd. in Oakland. https://chabotspace. org/events/events-listing/ Piedmont High School student Sage Mosley was an intern at Ames Research Center this past summer.

articles.text: Families can get started on Halloween festivities early by coming to see the Piedmont Middle School production of the musical The Addams Family Young@Part. The show is directed by Amy Moorhead. Celebrate the wackiness in every family with this musical comedy by composer and lyricist Andrew Lippa based on the book by Marshall Brickman and Rick Elice. Wednesday Addams, the ultimate princess of darkness, has grown up and fallen in love with a sweet, smart young man from a respectable family whom her parents have never met. In one fateful, hilarious night, secrets are disclosed, relationships are tested, and the Addams family must face up to the one horrible thing they’ve managed to avoid for generations: change. articles.text: From October 24 to November 7 members of the Piedmont 1st grade Girl Scout Daisy Troop, Troop 31318, will be collecting candy wrappers to recycle through the TerraCycle Zero Waste Program – and they have some big requests: 1. Trick-or-Treating When buying candy for trickor-treaters this year try choosing candy wrappers that are compostable, like Nerds boxes, paper Pixie Stix, and paper wrapped chocolates. 2. Saving Candy Wrappers Set up a bag in your home, maybe an old Amazon shipping bag, and start collecting the plastic candy wrappers that would otherwise end up in a landfill (or our parks and bay). 3. Recycling Bring your wrappers to the Troop 31318 TerraCycle Zero Waste collection bin outside of Mulberry’s Market from October 24th to November 7th. 4. Writing letters Does your favorite candy only have landfill destined wrapping? Write to the maker and ask them to change. As a community we can all help make a difference. Please show the 1st graders the difference we can make when we work together. A bin for candy wrappers will be in front of Mulberry’s Market for a collection drive by Piedmont Girl Scouts.

It is also an interesting idea to consider the City’s Master Plan for Housing to address what is potentially a hurdle to attract younger talent to PUSD. The California Healthy Kids Survey for 2021-22 revealed that only 73% of PHS students “agreed” or “strongly agreed” that there were “Caring Adults at School.” How can that be addressed and improved for the 27% who did not agree? (See the Board Background document on the survey from the school board meeting on Sept. 28, 2022: Simbli.eboardsolutions.com/Meetings/Attachment. aspx?S=36030373&AID=347899 &MID=15614.) 2. Teachers recently received a 7.5% raise, however they gave stated that this just keeps pace with inflation. Do you see the possibility of housing designated for teachers as part of the city’s master plan for additional housing? If so, how would you promote and implement that? SHIRLEY HOOI 1. “Caring Adults” at School? The California Healthy Kids Survey provides invaluable data as we seek to foster a caring, nurturing environment for our students. That said, in my professional experience thoughtful analysis is always necessary to transform data into actionable insights. As the School Board evaluates data to decide on actions, we must always be cognizant of four things 1) goals, 2) norms, 3) opportunity cost, and 4) ROI. In this case, the question implies PUSD’s goal should be 100% for Caring Adults in School … but should it? At the Elementary level, we’re already 10 points better than Alameda County (83% vs 73%)? Isn’t it a fairly strong statement that more than 4 in 5 students feel the Staff cares? Should we focus on improving this metric? LINDSAY THOMASSON 1. “Caring Adults” at School? We should start by reaching out to the students who reported that they didn’t feel that there were caring adults at school to understand why (like PUSD does with BESS Screener results). We should think beyond teachers and recognize that caring adults can be coaches, Wellness Center therapists, or one of the other adults we are fortunate to have supporting our students every day. There are a number of nonprofit organizations that partner with schools to provide evidence-based curriculum to help students connect to their teachers and peers through in-class activities, discussion topics, and beyond-class experiments; we could partner with one of these organizations to bring in their program during Academy classes. case for the importance of relationships, it gives teachers permission to focus on relationship building with their students. Isn’t it a fairly strong statement that more than 4 in 5 students feel the Staff cares? Should we focus on improving this metric? LINDSAY THOMASSON 1. “Caring Adults” at School? We should start by reaching out to the students who reported that they didn’t feel that there were caring adults at school to understand why (like PUSD does with BESS Screener results). We should think beyond teachers and recognize that caring adults can be coaches, Wellness Center therapists, or one of the other adults we are fortunate to have supporting our students every day. There are a number of nonprofit organizations that partner with schools to provide evidence-based curriculum to help students connect to their teachers and peers through in-class activities, discussion topics, and beyond-class experiments; we could partner with one of these organizations to bring in their program during Academy classes. By making an evidence-based case for the importance of relationships, it gives teachers permission to focus on relationship building with their students. We must empower and provide educators with the capacity and resources to build relationships with their students. 2. Teacher Housing in Piedmont? We have both a teacher crisis and a housing crisis; the two have intersected as we have heard many stories about teachers commuting long distances to work in Piedmont or living in substandard conditions. Teacher salaries in California have been unable RUCHI MEDHEKAR 1. “Caring Adults” at School? The sentiment amongst our kids has actually become more favorable (69% said they had a caring adult at school in ‘19-’20 versus 73% this year). That is a testament to the attention our teachers and staff have put into ensuring our students know they have resources to help them as they return to school. We could leverage the structure of the Academy period to improve and reach out to the quarter of students that don’t have a connection with a caring adult at school. It may not be a true problem for some of those respondents, however, who might have access to caring adults in their lives in other contexts. By ensuring that all kids know where to go if they need help, we can provide them with a robust support system that will serve them well. 2. Teacher Housing in Piedmont? Finding ways to make housing more affordable in our city for our teachers and staff would be an incredible boon for our city. Not only would it be a benefit in attracting and retaining talent in our district, we would also be building a true community where we live and work together. Housing in the Bay Area is expensive and takes up a material portion of our salaries - finding creative ways to solve for this expense would be tremendously helpful. I think we should consider how to extend housing to city employees as well, including our fire and police departments. If I were elected, I would partner with the district, the city, and our city council to understand how we could implement this idea in a reasonable time frame. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont resident and photographer, Steve Zirkelbach, took dozens of photos at Piedmont High’s Homecoming Dance on Saturday, October 1 which captured the electricity of the evening. As is tradition, the Homecoming dance in the Binks Rawlings gym punctuated the end of Homecoming Week (also known as Sprit Week) on campus. All students, from freshmen to seniors, were invited to dance the night away at the disco-themed party organized by Associated Student Body members. Four students were elected by their peers to the Homecoming Court and were presented with crowns at the student Homecoming rally on Friday. Seniors Milani Juarbe and Callan Mitchell were crowned as Homecoming Queen and King, and juniors Bauer Peterson and Shunji Hagashi were named Princess and Prince of the Homecoming Court on Friday, September 30. articles.text: Wildwood Dads Pumpkin Patch remains open through Oct. 30 Every pumpkin purchased at the Wildwood Dad Club’s Pumpkin Patch brings the dads one step closer to their goal of generating $30,000 in sales this year. Dads Club President Adam Fishman has been running the patch like a well-oiled machine this year and is egging on the Patch Papas on to sell, sell, sell. Everyone’s favorite game, guessing the weight of Giant Jack, the giant pumpkin that provides a centerpiece for the patch, is still open, and anyone can enter the contest. It’s not just kids trying to win the pumpkin with guesses at $1 each. Dads have been doing their own guesswork. Legendary Wildwood dad Adam Simons, who has had the winning guess twice in recent years, was on hand Friday The pumpkin delivery man, Kooky Kevin, was up to his normal shenanigans last week. He delivered a batch of enormous all-white pumpkins that came as a surprise to the dads. Pumpkins are still available in all shapes, colors, sizes and even culinary flavors this year. Stop by Coaches Field to have your pick from the following varieties: Yugoslavian finger fruit, sugar pie, “One Too Many,” fairytale, jarrahdale, peanut, American tondo, and knucklehead. To purchase pumpkins online, see: Wildwoodpumpkins.com the patch.
articles.title: Giant Jack weight still anyone’s guess

articles.text: The Highlanders’ boys’ water polo team continued its unbeaten run in the Western Alameda County Conference last week with an impressive 12-7 win against rival Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 11 at the Mills College pool. The victory improves Piedmont’s record to 15-4 overall and 7-0 in league. The team will likely be the No. 1 seed heading into the WACC Tournament at Encinal starting next Tuesday, October 25, with games through Saturday, October 29. Piedmont wraps up its regular season in a round robin tournament at Stevenson High in Pebble Beach this Saturday, October 22. “We’re trying to build up for league championships and NCS (North Coast Section playoffs). That was always our goal at the beginning of the season. We are in the driver’s seat, for sure, but we also need to make sure we maintain the pace at practice and work on little tweaks here and there,” said coach Rik Krumins. Piedmont jumped out to a comfortable 4-1 lead by the end of the first quarter with O’Dowd, and went up 7-3 by halftime. They kept a four-goal advantage through the third quarter to lead 9-5 and closed out with three more goals in the fourth, 12-7. In the first quarter, Finn Burke scored the first two goals of the game in less than a minute. O’Dowd cut the deficit to 2-1, but George Stein made it 3-1 with a goal during a man-advantage with 2:05 remaining. PHS then killed two separate penalties before drawing a 5-meter penalty with just four seconds left, allowing Peter Krumins to make it 4-1. BOD narrowed the score to 4-3 at the 3:33 mark in the second quarter, but it was their last goal in the first half. Hayden Jahn scored with 2:44 to play, and scored again during a man-advantage with 33 seconds left. With four seconds left in the half, Quincy Scherman launched a goal into net. In the third quarter, Piedmont’s Declan Linnane scored three seconds after gaining a penalty at the 6:07 mark, 8-3. BOD then converted a man-advantage opportunity with 4:55 left and scored once more with 2:43 to go, making it 8-5. PHS drew another exclusion penalty in the dying seconds, leading to Daniel Banin scoring with two seconds left, 9-5. Photo by Nancy Brahm Daniel Banin had a goal, assist, and steal on O’Dowd. Krumins scored 22 seconds into the fourth quarter to make it 10-5. BOD scored with 4:26 left in the game, 10-6, but it took Stein just 20 seconds and scored once more with a man-advantage with 3:17 to play for PHS’ final goal. Bishop O’Dowd tacked one on with 41 seconds remaining. Final stats include: Stein led the way with three goals. Krumins and Burke scored twice and had one steal, Jahn scored twice as well. Linnane had a goal, two assists, and two steals. Banin had a goal, assist, and steal. Scherman scored a goal. Goalie Dariush Kashani had 10 saves and a steal. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls tennis team claimed a big 4-3 win over league rivals Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 11. The victory puts PHS in first place of the Western Alameda County Conference with a 7-0 league record, and on pace for its first WACC title since 2018. “It was like déjà vu. We defeated O’Dowd 4-3; just like we defeated them at the California Tennis Classic (in early September in Fresno), and the same score when we defeated Berkeley the previous week. We are now No. 1 in the WACC League, but we can’t rest. We will be playing all the Foothill teams again, and they were all close matches before, so we need to keep getting better,” said coach Jim Landes. PHS still must face challenging league matches with Alameda, Berkeley, Castro Valley, and O’Dowd once more before the end of the season. With wins over each school, Piedmont would accomplish their first undefeated banner year since the last title in 2018. The Highlanders famously held the longest undefeated streak against league opponents in California high school tennis at 19-years long from 2000-2018. The school also won five consecutive D2 NCS Team Championship titles during that stretch from 2013-2017. PHS could’ve made it six consecutive in 2018 as the No. 1 seed, but smoke from the wildfire in Paradise in late November and rain in early December canceled the tournament. Piedmont’s final three matches of the regular season will be at Alameda on Thursday, October 20, hosting Berkeley on Tuesday, October 25, and then at O’Dowd on Thursday, October 27. 4-3 win over Bishop O’Dowd Against Bishop O’Dowd, Piedmont won all three doubles matches and took one of four at singles to claim the win. At singles, No. 1 starter Tanya Kononova continued her winning streak with a 6-2, 6-0 win. It marked her seventh consecutive win. At No. 2 was Anne Jumper falling 6-1, 6-1, while Carolina Romanczuk lost 6-2, 7-5 at No. 3. Annika Gilliland had a narrow two sets at No. 4 but lost 7-5, 7-5. Over to doubles, Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini continued their strong play at the No. 1 spot, winning 7-5, 6-2. They have now won five consecutive matches as Piedmont’s top doubles team. “I think we’re really good at picking each other up in our low moments. We know how to stay positive when we play together; it’s really important to have a doubles partner who can take things seriously but also be really flexible and supportive,” said Bini. “Michaela is just great. She’s funny and we can make each other laugh even when we hit a ball way too hard out onto the street. We can look at each other, laugh it off, and know everything will be fine,” said LaForte. At No. 2 was Emma Eisemon and Ceclilia DeFazio winning in three sets, 6-2, 4-6, 6-3, while the freshman pair of Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum won 6-2, 6-2 at No. 3. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team lost 7-3 to Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 11 at Mills College in Oakland, snapping a fourgame winning streak by the Highlanders. It was a close for three quarters with O’Dowd holding a 4-3 lead to start the fourth period. The loss brings Piedmont’s record to 6-9 overall and 1-4 in league with one match remaining in its regular season before the start of the Western Alameda County Conference tournament from Tuesday, October 25 through Saturday, October 29 at the Encinal HS pool in Alameda. The Dragons led 2-0 by the end of the first quarter and kept the two-goal advantage by halftime, 3-1. Piedmont ate away at the lead in the third quarter and closed the score to 4-3 but couldn’t maintain the offensive fluidity in the fourth, falling 7-3. O’Dowd came out of the gate hot, scoring its first goal within 26 seconds into the game after winning the opening sprint. Piedmont’s goalie Friedie Schickedanz did well to record two saves in the remaining time, including a pivotal stop of a penalty situation, but the Dragons scored on a breakaway with 58 seconds left in the quarter. In the second quarter, Katarina Melian scored with 56 seconds left in the half, but Bishop O’Dowd answered just 14 seconds later on its next possession. Prior to then, Odessa Dando recorded a steal and drew an exclusion penalty, which led to Melian taking a shot attempt with 5:30 to play, but her ball went to the right of net. Piedmont started the third quarter strongly by drawing an exclusion and scored four seconds later when Melian launched a long-range shot into the net, cutting the deficit to 3-2. However, the Dragons scored with a long shot of its own with six minutes to play. PHS answered 13 seconds later on its next possession Photos by Nancy Brahm Rosie Feldman scored once against the Dragons. with Dando assisting Rosie Feldman on a close-range goal to make it 4-3, but it was the last time they’d get on the score sheet. In the remaining minutes of the third period, Piedmont gained four exclusion penalties against BOD but the Dragon goalie made critical saves and some shots went wide of the net. In the fourth quarter O’Dowd converted a 6-on-5 opportunity with 5:26 left in the game, extending the lead to 5-3. From there, BOD scored at the 3:42 mark by way of a breakaway goal, 6-3, and then tacked on one more with just 39 seconds to play. Final stats include: Melian had two goals, while Feldman had one. Dando had two steals and an assist. Tuesday vs. Alameda Piedmont played a match with Alameda on Tuesday, October 18 at the Encinal pool for its final regular season match of the season. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-9 overall, 1-4 league) is set to play in the WACC Tournament at Encinal. The first round game is on Tuesday, October 25 with semifinals on Thursday, October 27 and finals on Saturday, October 29. Odessa Dando looks for a pass. She had two steals and an assist against O’Dowd. Piedmont are set to play in the WACC Tournament from October 25-29.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team returned to action on Friday, October 15 after a three-week absence, and fall 22-14 to Bishop O’Dowd. It marked a return to action for the football program after canceling the remaining 5 varsity games on its schedule following a game on September 23. “It was awesome to play a game again. It was our first game in three weeks; the kids have been antsy just waiting to get out there. The kids were super excited and were working hard all week in practice. It’s a great group,” said JV coach Bradley Smet, who also serves as the high school Athletic Director. The JV squad inherited a few underclassmen on the varsity team. “We were able to bring some of the kids down [from varsity to JV]. The sophomores including Brayden Hong and Derek Schleuning as juniors, so we were able to split players up more offensively and defensively. We didn’t have to play all of our kids both ways and we were able to rotate players more. It gave an opportunity for kids to play and exert their energy in their primary role,” explained Smet. The Highlanders trailed 14-0 by the end of the first quarter after allowing a kickoff return for a touchdown, followed by O’Dowd scoring on a 65-yard touchdown pass. “They had two big plays at the beginning of the game. Aside from those, I thought we did a great job controlling the game. That was the downfall in our last game against St. Mary’s, where we suffered several turnovers. Staff Photos Sophomore Tommy Ashton, who had been on the varsity team, scored a touchdown and a made a two-point conversion for the JV football team in its game with Bishop O’Dowd on October 15. JV coach Bradley Smet gives a play call to quarterback Brandon Dicke. Miguel Long goes high for a touchdown reception against O’Dowd. We asked the team to take care of the ball and that’s what they did,” said Smet. Piedmont rallied in the fourth quarter to bring itself within one possession. With 8:16 left in the game, quarterback Brandon Dicke connected with Miguel Long in the end zone pm a 20-yard touchdown pass to make it a 14-6 game following a failed two-point conversion. The Dragons scored with 3:50 left in the game after a long pass to the one-yard line and then punching the ball across. But on Piedmont’s next possession, the Highlanders churned downfield with long runs led by Ashton and Cash Panico, leading to Ashton powering his way on a five-yard carry across the goal line, shouldering his way over an attempted tackle. He also converted a twopoint conversion to make it 22-14. “It was great to be back out there. It wasn’t the result we wanted, but we had a lot of fun,” said Ashton. But Piedmont wasn’t done. On the ensuing kickoff, PHS recovered its onside kick on the right sideline to gain possession and be in great field position and with enough time to tie the game. But on a second down at the 30-yard line, Dicke quarterback suffered a shot to the ribs and had to leave the game. Its once promising drive ended at the 28-yard line. “We caught them by surprise on the onside kick. Albert Bellingrath kicked the ball and Long went streaking down the sideline to get it. They executed their jobs perfectly,” said Smet. The JV team continues with three more scheduled games, at St. Patrick in Vallejo this Friday, October 21, at Tennyson in Haywards on Thursday, October 27, and at home against Kennedy on Friday, November 4. articles.text: Piedmont High School is pushing forward with Junior Varsity football after a tumultuous cancellation of the five varsity games remaining on its schedule. JV will continue, but due to a diminished roster and injuries, the varsity season was terminated following a game on September 23. The JV team played its first game in three weeks on Friday, October 14, but there was no varsity game. Although JV head coach Bradley Smet, who also is the school’s athletic director, was calling the offense. Varsity head coach Jordan Seiden has been taking the reins at practice. “Once we decided to make the move with varsity, we talked about bringing our [varsity] staff down to JV and starting the transition for those players who will be getting varsity experience next year. We’re getting them used to our system and expectations. We definitely want to run the same system on both levels (JV and varsity), so we’re building the culture and a true program,” said Seiden. Defensive coordinator Mike Dixon called the plays in Friday’s game and in future games, offensive coordinator Kerry Griffin will take control. “The kids are using the same terminology and all those things, so we thought the natural progression would be for us to be working with JV as a unit. Our defensive coordinator is running the JV defense with assistance of the other coaches who were there. Mike Dixon is running the offense starting this week, last week with coach Smet,” said Seiden. Most of Piedmont’s varsity lineup included sophomores and juniors under Seiden, where a large focus of attention was developing players. That undoubtedly becomes an even greater emphasis going forward on JV, allowing Seiden to learn even more players to his incumbent varsity team in 2023. “It’s been nice having time to work with the team before playing O’Dowd. We are still going through the transition of getting to know each other, I tell the team that it’s almost like starting over again. We have a chance to get a leg-up on next year by getting together this year. We’re keeping the focus on developing and getting better; the focus of JV is more about developing and growth rather than wins and losses, said Seiden. pages.text: 14 Wednesday, October 19, 2022 JV football team falls by 1 touchdown to O’Dowd By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team returned to action on Friday, October 15 after a three-week absence, and fall 22-14 to Bishop O’Dowd. It marked a return to action for the football program after canceling the remaining 5 varsity games on its schedule following a game on September 23. “It was awesome to play a game again. It was our first game in three weeks; the kids have been antsy just waiting to get out there. The kids were super excited and were working hard all week in practice. It’s a great group,” said JV coach Bradley Smet, who also serves as the high school Athletic Director. The JV squad inherited a few underclassmen on the varsity team. “We were able to bring some of the kids down [from varsity to JV]. The sophomores including Brayden Hong and Derek Schleuning as juniors, so we were able to split players up more offensively and defensively. We didn’t have to play all of our kids both ways and we were able to rotate players more. It gave an opportunity for kids to play and exert their energy in their primary role,” explained Smet. The Highlanders trailed 14-0 by the end of the first quarter after allowing a kickoff return for a touchdown, followed by O’Dowd scoring on a 65-yard touchdown pass. “They had two big plays at the beginning of the game. Aside from those, I thought we did a great job controlling the game. That was the downfall in our last game against St. Mary’s, where we suffered several turnovers. Staff Photos Sophomore Tommy Ashton, who had been on the varsity team, scored a touchdown and a made a two-point conversion for the JV football team in its game with Bishop O’Dowd on October 15. JV coach Bradley Smet gives a play call to quarterback Brandon Dicke. Miguel Long goes high for a touchdown reception against O’Dowd. We asked the team to take care of the ball and that’s what they did,” said Smet. Piedmont rallied in the fourth quarter to bring itself within one possession. With 8:16 left in the game, quarterback Brandon Dicke connected with Miguel Long in the end zone pm a 20-yard touchdown pass to make it a 14-6 game following a failed two-point conversion. The Dragons scored with 3:50 left in the game after a long pass to the one-yard line and then punching the ball across. But on Piedmont’s next possession, the Highlanders churned downfield with long runs led by Ashton and Cash Panico, leading to Ashton powering his way on a five-yard carry across the goal line, shouldering his way over an attempted tackle. He also converted a twopoint conversion to make it 22-14. “It was great to be back out there. It wasn’t the result we wanted, but we had a lot of fun,” said Ashton. But Piedmont wasn’t done. On the ensuing kickoff, PHS recovered its onside kick on the right sideline to gain possession and be in great field position and with enough time to tie the game. But on a second down at the 30-yard line, Dicke quarterback suffered a shot to the ribs and had to leave the game. Its once promising drive ended at the 28-yard line. “We caught them by surprise on the onside kick. Albert Bellingrath kicked the ball and Long went streaking down the sideline to get it. They executed their jobs perfectly,” said Smet. The JV team continues with three more scheduled games, at St. Patrick in Vallejo this Friday, October 21, at Tennyson in Haywards on Thursday, October 27, and at home against Kennedy on Friday, November 4. articles.text: Piedmont’s cross-country team raced on the trails at Point Pinole Regional Shoreline on Wednesday, October 12 for its second Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season The boys’ team finished third of 10 schools while the girls were fourth out of nine teams. “As we get to our last meets of the season, we inevitably start calculating results and sometimes get too caught up in a frenzy of beating certain teams. At Point Pinole, we were pleased to see a large number of improvements. This is only the second year that the league has raced on this course,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. The boys’ team finished four points behind Bishop O’Dowd, 64-60, while Berkeley blitzed the field with a team score of 31. Christian Taylor (2507) was third of 91 runners with a time of 16:05.35 in a league meet at Point Pinole. Jamie Schwarz (1683) and Skylar Best (1656) placed fourth and ninth in the recent league meet. Running without Senior Christian Taylor led PHS by finishing third in a field of 91 runners with a time of 16:05. Behind him was classmate Parker Long in fourth in 16:09.84. The team was without lead runner Xander Schulte-Sasse, who placed third overall in the GOAT Invitational in Hercules on October 1. Junior Julien Lee was ninth with a time of 16:33.93, senior Alex Ware in 22nd place in 17:21.40, and sophomore Evan Byun 29th in 17:36.02. Junior Jamie Schwarz led the girls’ team, placing fourth out of 65 runners with a time of 19:52.9. She has finished in the top five in all her race this season. Freshman standout Skylar Best was ninth with a time of 20:25.82. next came a trio of up-and-coming freshman runners. Cora Chun (28th, 21:39.12), Elia Kwong (30th, 21:51.72), and Quincy Antaya in 33rd in 22:08.41. The girls team also was without one of its top runners, Josie Oesterer, who ran a time of 19:51.5 at the league meet on September 21. NEXT UP Piedmont is set to race in another league meet today, Wednesday, October 19, at Oyster Bay Regional Park at 4:00 p.m. Later this week, the squad heads to the prestigious Mt. Sac Invitational on Friday, October 21 in Walnut in Southern California. Elia Kwong, a freshman, finished in 21:51.72 at the league meet.

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California will host its 28th annual Dia de los Muertos Celebration this Sunday, October 23 from 12 noon to 4 p.m. The museum, in collaboration with OMCA’s El Día de Muertos Volunteer Community Committee, explores the culture and heritage of Latin America through music, dance, food, and art. Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is a celebration and appreciation of life and death practiced mainly in Mexico. Visitors will enjoy performances by Ballet Folklorico Mexicano and Mariachi Femenil Orgullo Mexicano, an all-female Mariachi band from the Bay Area. Traditional indigenous dance will be performed by Danza Azteca Nahui Ehekatl. Celebrating Dia de los Muertos at Oakland Museum of California with music, dance, food and art. View the community offerings at the ofrenda (altar) and explore the art of repujado (embossing). The festivities will take place between 12 p.m. and 4 p.m. This is a family-friendly event. Visit https://museumca.org/dia-de-losmuertos/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Oakland Museum celebrates Dia de los Muertos this Sunday

articles.text: Indecent is based on the real-life events of Sholem Asch’s Broadway debut The God of Vengeance. San Francisco Playhouse is celebrating its 20th season with a performance of Indecent, Paula Vogel’s new play based on the real-life events of Sholem Asch’s Broadway debut of The God of Vengeance. Although many consider Asch’s work to be a seminal work of Jewish culture, it is also viewed by some as libelous. The play is being performed at SF Playhouse through November 5. “We were lucky enough to be on hand when Paula Vogel’s Indecent opened on Broadway five years ago, and being huge fans of hers already, and galvanized by the production, we began angling to present the play’s Bay Area premiere immediately,” said San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English. “At the time we were a long shot due to strong interest from bigger companies, but after a two-year pandemic and catastrophic changes in the American theatre, a door opened five years later for us to present Indecent.” The play is directed by Susi Damilano, with music direction by Dmitri Gaskin and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The cast includes Dean Linnard, Billy Cohen, Rachel Botchan, and Rivka Borek. The show is co-produced with the Yiddish Theatre Ensemble and features a klezmer music score. “It is both a love song to the Ashkenazi Jewish culture spanning 50 years and a love song to the theatre. It is an odyssey that spins us from Warsaw to Berlin, to NY Yiddish theatre, to Broadway and back to Warsaw as the tumultuous and tragic history of the early 20th Century unfolds around the play within our play,” English said. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/ sfph/get-tickets/. The concert will conclude with the lively “Monti Czardas.” A light reception to meet the artists will follow. articles.text: Zheng Chongbin’s large art installation, I Look for the Sky, is on view now at San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. The installation uses transparency and light to explore how ephemeral changes can alter the viewer’s perception. The exhibition is located in the museum’s Bogart Court. “Art has always been a pathway to this fuzzy world. It’s full of probabilities and chance – and so it was, working on this installation,” Chongbin said. “The assembled fragmented pieces were never about fixing the object itself, but rather about the shifting relationship among the fragments, a resonance, a natural chemistry. Culture and nature need to share the same space; society, all living beings, this physical planet, this earth, are interconnected.” Chongbin is a Bay Area-based artist trained in classical Chinese figurative painting who studied performance, installation, and conceptual art at San Francisco Art Institute. Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/zhengchongbin-i-look-for-the-sky-2/ to purchase tickets. The large exhibit, I Look for the Sky, is on view in the Bogart Court at San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum.
articles.title: Chongbin’s I Look for the Sky on view now at Asian Art Museum

articles.text: A leader in symphonic innovation and imagination now for six decades, the Oakland Symphony launched its first full post-pandemic season on October 14 with the first of its music-director candidates out front. And, of course, with an innovative program. Through countless setbacks, the ensemble keeps emerging again and again like a phoenix from the ashes; its struggles remain a challenge for the future. Has any ensemble suffered greater adversity? It went bankrupt after the off-season death (accidental drowning) of its highly talented 32-year-old maestro Calvin Simmons precisely 40 years ago. He had been feted as the first Black conductor of any major U.S. orchestra. The more recent Oakland Symphony music director, the exemplary Michael Morgan (also Black), died last year at the age of only 63, having served here indefatigably since 1991. Given the large Oakland Black population, these men were a welcome fit for the community as they presented a very broad-ranging repertory that was rarely predictable. Local commemorations of Morgan are well-deserved. But the charismatic Simmons remains a bit marginalized. Both made immense contributions, each in his own way. And now the new era, with the lead-off batter (it’s still baseball season) Ankush Kumar Bahl as the podium guest, marking the orchestra’s resumption of a normal, full-season schedule. Bahl was a Bay Area product of Indian descent now running the Omaha Symphony and vying for the Oakland directorship. Nurtured by some very prominent conductors, he has a secure stick technique demonstrated in two demanding contemporary works. He is also one of the most adept annotators that the Paramount Theater podium has heard in recent years. Chen Yi’s The Golden Flute Flute virtuoso Demarre McGill performed with Oakland Symphony In its season-opening concert on October 14. was a priceless virtuosity vehicle for flute virtuoso Demarre McGill, the guest soloist, and the orchestra. Despite his modest-size frame, McGill is one powerful flutist with extraordinary breath control, in turns both whimsical and canary-like, able to modulate tones like gentle swells with breath alone. His bird effects were swooping and swarming unerringly, all while imbuing this Western orchestra with techniques from China. They emanate from composer Yi, a remarkable émigré woman, now 69, who had managed to smuggle her violin and clandestine Bach music to the work farms during the Cultural Revolution, “to inspire the peasants working the fields,” more or less as Mao would have it back then. (Bach? With Mao?) Moving on from the cadence that brought down the house, McGill appended James Lee’s Principal Brothers, an unaccompanied showpiece encore. Bahl followed with Berlioz’s Symphonie Fantastique, often cited as the very first romantic symphony. As the personnel here in their six-concert classical series play few romantics, the start was too detached for comfort, like a vintage table that could use some regluing. But the middle movement depicting the shepherd horn calls across the mountains was beautifully wrought by Bahl and cohorts. Buoyed by the sinuous oboe solos of Andrea Plesnarski, the movement lifted up this entire programmatic symphony through the gallows scene, the beheading, and the witches’ sabbath toward an effusive celebration of death by the morbid hero of the symphony. Notable among the sections of this enlarged Berlioz orchestra were the violas and the harp pairing. Three bass players were too few, but on the other hand you had to admire the rarity of paired tubas. Named after Beethoven’s motto “Fate Now Conquers,” composer Carlos Simon, 36, also quoted some harmonies from Beethoven’s Seventh for the brief but profoundly accented curtain-raiser. MUSIC NOTES Yet another Oakland musical luminary, Bob Hughes (Robert Grove Hughes), passed away this summer at 91. He had been a true jack of all trades, as bassoonist, conductor and composer. A longtime collaborator of composer Lou Harrison, conductor Hughes had also founded the Oakland Youth Orchestra and was credited as composer on the Disney film Never Cry Wolf. Piedmont resident Paul Hertelendy also writes for the classical-music site www.artsSF.com .
articles.title: Battling Symphonic adversity – and winning

articles.text: Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen San Francisco Symphony will perform a Halloween-inspired program of music across the Bay at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus this Friday, October 21. The concert will be led by Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen. Included in the program are three “spooky” works – Mussorgsky’s I, Liszt’s Totentanz (Dance of Death) performed by pianist Bertrand Chamayou, and Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, Op. 14. This concert is part of San Francisco Symphony’s fortnight of Halloween programming, beginning October 20. Tickets are available online at calperformances.org or by phone at (510) 642-9988.
articles.title: SF Symphony to perform Halloween-inspired concert at Zellerbach on Friday

articles.text: City Council member Betsy Andersen makes cameo appearance in Ferdinand the Bull Piedmont’s hometown orchestra will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday afternoon, November 6, at 4 p.m. Conducted by Martha Stoddard and Sue Crum, the orchestra will perform the rarely heard Overture to Johann Albrecht’s comedy Der Teufel als Hydraulicus, composed by Franz Schubert when he was just 14. Other music includes the delightful Romanian Dances, by Bela Bartok, and Mozart’s orchestral masterpiece, Symphony No. 40 in G minor, composed during some of the artist’s darkest days. pages.text: Wednesday, October 19, 2022 17 Battling Symphonic adversity – and winning By Paul Hertelendy A leader in symphonic innovation and imagination now for six decades, the Oakland Symphony launched its first full post-pandemic season on October 14 with the first of its music-director candidates out front. And, of course, with an innovative program. Through countless setbacks, the ensemble keeps emerging again and again like a phoenix from the ashes; its struggles remain a challenge for the future. Has any ensemble suffered greater adversity? It went bankrupt after the off-season death (accidental drowning) of its highly talented 32-year-old maestro Calvin Simmons precisely 40 years ago. He had been feted as the first Black conductor of any major U.S. orchestra. The more recent Oakland Symphony music director, the exemplary Michael Morgan (also Black), died last year at the age of only 63, having served here indefatigably since 1991. Given the large Oakland Black population, these men were a welcome fit for the community as they presented a very broad-ranging repertory that was rarely predictable. Local commemorations of Morgan are well-deserved. But the charismatic Simmons remains a bit marginalized. Both made immense contributions, each in his own way. And now the new era, with the lead-off batter (it’s still baseball season) Ankush Kumar Bahl as the podium guest, marking the orchestra’s resumption of a normal, full-season schedule. Bahl was a Bay Area product of Indian descent now running the Omaha Symphony and vying for the Oakland directorship. Nurtured by some very prominent conductors, he has a secure stick technique demonstrated in two demanding contemporary works. He is also one of the most adept annotators that the Paramount Theater podium has heard in recent years. Chen Yi’s The Golden Flute Flute virtuoso Demarre McGill performed with Oakland Symphony In its season-opening concert on October 14. was a priceless virtuosity vehicle for flute virtuoso Demarre McGill, the guest soloist, and the orchestra. Despite his modest-size frame, McGill is one powerful flutist with extraordinary breath control, in turns both whimsical and canary-like, able to modulate tones like gentle swells with breath alone. His bird effects were swooping and swarming unerringly, all while imbuing this Western orchestra with techniques from China. They emanate from composer Yi, a remarkable émigré woman, now 69, who had managed to smuggle her violin and clandestine Bach music to the work farms during the Cultural Revolution, “to inspire the peasants working the fields,” more or less as Mao would have it back then. (Bach? With Mao?) Moving on from the cadence that brought down the house, McGill appended James Lee’s Principal Brothers, an unaccompanied showpiece encore. Bahl followed with Berlioz’s Symphonie Fantastique, often cited as the very first romantic symphony. As the personnel here in their six-concert classical series play few romantics, the start was too detached for comfort, like a vintage table that could use some regluing. But the middle movement depicting the shepherd horn calls across the mountains was beautifully wrought by Bahl and cohorts. Buoyed by the sinuous oboe solos of Andrea Plesnarski, the movement lifted up this entire programmatic symphony through the gallows scene, the beheading, and the witches’ sabbath toward an effusive celebration of death by the morbid hero of the symphony. Notable among the sections of this enlarged Berlioz orchestra were the violas and the harp pairing. Three bass players were too few, but on the other hand you had to admire the rarity of paired tubas. Named after Beethoven’s motto “Fate Now Conquers,” composer Carlos Simon, 36, also quoted some harmonies from Beethoven’s Seventh for the brief but profoundly accented curtain-raiser. MUSIC NOTES Yet another Oakland musical luminary, Bob Hughes (Robert Grove Hughes), passed away this summer at 91. He had been a true jack of all trades, as bassoonist, conductor and composer. A longtime collaborator of composer Lou Harrison, conductor Hughes had also founded the Oakland Youth Orchestra and was credited as composer on the Disney film Never Cry Wolf. Piedmont resident Paul Hertelendy also writes for the classical-music site www.artsSF.com . articles.text: The popular Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy exhibition at Legion of Honor, of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, has been extended to November 27 due to popular demand. The fashion exhibit features the extraordinary designs of Chinese couture designer Guo Pei, who is widely considered China’s first couturier. More than 80 works over the past two decades will be on display, many of them were shown on Beijing and Paris runways. Pei is known for her craftsmanship, embroidery, and unconventional dressmaking techniques. “As a creator and artist, there is no greater honor than to share my creativity with a wider audience,” the artist said. “I hope that, through the artistry of couture and universal language of art, that it will foster cross-cultural appreciation, connections, and ideas.” The exhibition drew over 130,000 visitors in the first 18 weeks. Legion of Honor then extended Guo Pei’s exhibition for 12 more weeks. “Our visitors’ response to Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy has been absolutely extraordinary, and we are delighted that the exhibition’s Chinese couture designer Guo Pei. extension through Thanksgiving will enable more people to experience Guo Pei’s artistry,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Installed in our special exhibition galleries, and amid our holdings of European Art, Guo Pei’s designs encompass rich details both infused with references to a range of cultural traditions and executed over thousands of hours. This presentation represents a singular opportunity to experience exquisite designs that invoke and encourage transcultural dialogue.” Visit https://legionof honor. famsf.org/guo-pei for more information and to purchase tickets to the exhibition.

articles.text: An exhibit by husband and wife artists Claire and David Cunningham will continue at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, October 23, from 3-5 p.m. The works in watercolor and oils are by Claire and gouache and acrylic for David’s paintings. Many of the works come from their outings in the high Sierras where they regularly hike and take their painting materials and easels in backpacks. Often the smaller works are used to create bigger paintings, giving the artists the opportunity to explore their subjects on a larger scale. This show also has local themes such as seascapes from the Monterey Peninsula, Bay Area gardens, some still life works, and a few portraits. “We find working together in wild areas with rich landscape to be a transcendent experience. We feel very fortunate to be able to explore and create from the incredible beauty of California,” said David. Claire is a MA graduate from California College of Arts & Crafts in Oakland and has taught both at CCAC and at Skyline College. David holds both a BFA and an MFA. For more information, see their website: www.cunninghampaintings.com. Asilomar Dunes, 14x18 Carmel Winter Sunset, 24X30

Sundays, October 23, 3:00–5:00 p.m. Cunningham Art Exhibition This show includes landscapes of the Sierras: Yosemite and the Plumas lakes basin; seascapes from the Monterey coast, Rockridge and Ben Lomond gardens, and still life paintings. The artists, husband and wife David and Claire Cunningham often hike into the high country and paint smaller works, which they then expand into larger pieces at home where they are able to extend the range of colors and material on a bigger scale. The concert will conclude with the lively “Monti Czardas.” A light reception to meet the artists follows. A plucked string orchestra with 15- 25 members playing instruments of the mandolin family (mandolin, mandola and mandocello), as well as guitar, viola da gamba and double bass, their musicianship and style have pleased Piedmont audiences many times.
