articles.text: A scene from Touching the Void. Touching the Void is a taut, compelling docudrama, directed by Kevin Macdonald, and based on a book of the same name written by Joe Simpson. The film recounts Simpson’s (Brendan Mackey) and Simon Yates’ (Nicholas Aaron), 1985 successful ascent of the never climbed West Face of the 21,000- foot Siula Grande peak in the Peruvian Andes. Simpson and Yates, both experienced mountaineers, having reached the summit, confidently begin their decent by way of the North Ridge. Unexpectedly the weather turns stormy and not long after leaving the summit Yates plummets some 4,500 feet down an icy slope, stopped only by his climbing rope and ax. After the fall, they decide to bivouac high on the peak, and the next morning resume their downward climb. It was during that decent that the film takes an ominous turn when Simpson unexpectedly drops over an ice cliff and finds himself dangling over a deep crevasse, still roped to Yates, 300 feet above him. Yates, feeling the rope go suddenly taut, digs the heels of his boots into the snow and ice; however, he soon begins to lose both grip and purchase and realizes that if he falls he will also go over the ledge. It is then that he makes a fateful decision and cuts the rope, and it is that act which literally separates the two for the rest of the film. As a result of Yates cutting him loose, Simpson falls into the deep, dark, crevasse, landing on a narrow ledge, his broken leg so painful he passes out. What was a climbing challenge has suddenly become a story of survival, and Simpson’s situation is now starkly untenable. He realizes that Yates most likely thinks he is dead and if he is to prevail, he must do so alone. And so begins his long ordeal, one of impossible odds. First he must find a way off the narrow ledge and out of his icy prison, wondering how, with a shattered leg, will ever find his way back down the face of a massive glacier and back to the base camp. This docudrama is an exceptionally excellent reenactment, and delivers sustained tension, excitement, and intensity, coupled with moments that seem all but hopeless. Touching the Void. Docudrama. Directed by Kevin Macdonald. Cast: Brendan Mackey as Joe Simpson, and Nicholas Aaron as Simon Yates. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated R. Released in 2003. Now streaming on Prime/AMC+/ Apple tv.

articles.text: A scene from Dreamworks’ Shark Tale. Review by Chris Honoré Shark Tale is a Dreamworks animated feature starring a bluestreak cleaner wrasse fish named Oscar (Will Smith) and a timid vegetarian shark named Lenny (Jack Black). This odd-couple hangs out in the Southside reef. Oscar dreams of becoming rich and famous while working at the local Whale Wash, and Lenny has to deal with his mobbed up family, led by his dad, Don Edward Lino, who worries that his son, a shark, prefers not to eat fish. The Don decides that Lenny needs some gangster mentoring and assigns the task to his older son, tough-talking Frankie (Michael Imperoli). When Oscar reports to work, he is called into the office of his boss, Sykes (Martin Scorsese), a puffer fish, who not only owns the Whale Wash, but on the side is a loan shark to whom Oscar owes money. Sykes tells Oscar that it’s time to pay the debt – some 5,000 clams – the next day, or else. Oscar, broke, is rescued by his best friend Angie (Renee Zellweger) who gives him a shiny pink pearl, which Oscar quickly pawns. The next day, Oscar brings the money to the racetrack where he intends to pay Sykes, but hears that there is a sure thing sea horse running, named Lucky Day, and he bets all of his cash to win. It’s an exciting race with Lucky in the lead; however, at the last moment, just before the finish line, Lucky trips and loses – and so does Oscar. Sykes, hearing that Oscar cannot pay him, sends two of his enforcers, Ernie and Bernie (Ziggy Marley and Doug E. Doug), Jamaican jellyfish, to deal with Oscar. And so we’re introduced to Oscar who is always on the verge of trouble. He happens to be in the vicinity of an anchor, which is dropped and hits Frankie, killing him. Suddenly the locals of Southside reef are referring to Oscar as a “shark slayer,” a tale that he doesn’t dispute. After all, fame is fame, and he enjoys his new reputation. Of course, there are lots of machinations taking place, with behind-the-scenes double-dealing, chases and plotting, all involving Angie, Lenny, and a seductive female Lion fish named Lola (Angelina Jolie). She gives Oscar a big kiss, making Angie jealous. And then there is, Don Lino, who believes Oscar killed Frankie and is seeking revenge. At one point he sends his left-hand man, Luca (Vincent Pastore), an octopus, to track down Oscar. Finally, Oscar steps forward and confesses that it was an anchor that killed Frankie and not him. Lenny and Don Lino reconcile, and Oscar becomes the manager of the Whale Wash. It’s all a comedy of errors that the kids will enjoy, highlighted by the jive-talking Oscar. Shark Tale. Dreamworks animation. Directed by Bibo Bergeron & Vicky Jenson. With voices of Will Smith, Robert DeNiro, Renee Zellweger. 1 hr. 30 min. Rated PG. Released in 2004. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: The California Air Resources Board (CARB) recently approved a first-in-the-nation plan to set zero-emissions standards for space and water heaters, effectively banning the sale of gas-powered furnaces and water heaters by 2030. Buildings will be required to install zero emissions alternatives such as energy efficient electric heat pumps. The proposal, approved late last month, is part of a larger plan to cut greenhouse gas emissions and meet federal air quality standards. The full text of the legislation is available at: Arb.ca.gov/ sites/default/files/2022-08/2022_ State_SIP_Strategy.pdf CARB’s plan directs state agencies to draft legislation to phase out gas-fueled heaters and will be subject to a final vote in 2025. The plan also includes further emissions reduction measures for trucks, medium and heavy-duty vehicles, and consumer products. The goal of the plan is to improve air quality and reduce nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions that contribute to particulate matter and ground-level ozone (otherwise known as smog). Control of NOx emissions is critical to improving air quality in California. Currently, more than half of Californians reside in areas that exceed the federal heath-based ozone standards. Low-income and disadvantaged communities are more likely to be impacted by high ozone levels. CARB’s latest plan will speed up the Golden State’s transition away from fossil fuels to cleaner forms of energy. In Piedmont the City’s Sustainability Division is actively pursuing ways to reduce emissions and transition to electric appliances and vehicles. Earlier this year, the City approved replacing all remaining gas-powered water heaters in City facilities with electric heat pump water heaters at no cost to the City. In the spring, the City Council directed that the new Piedmont Community Pool, scheduled to be completed in 2024, be designed as an all-electric facility. The entire facility will be electrified through a combination of electric heat pumps, solar panels, and integration with the clean electrical grid. The City is currently developing an electrification rebate pilot program that will provide incentives for residents to replace polluting gas appliances with clean electric alternatives. Together, these efforts will lessen our carbon footprint and improve our air quality. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions on electrification, plant-based eating, or hiking.
articles.title: California aims to ban gas water heaters, furnaces by 2030

articles.text: Mount Veeder is an American Viticultural Area (AVA) among the Mayacaymas Mountains west of Napa and Yountville. The mountain was named after Peter Veeder a Dutch Presbyterian minister who was one of the first non-natives to explore the area. The area has been producing wines since the 1860’s and is the only hillside appellation in Napa Valley that adjoins the cool, bayside Carneros, benefiting from the cooling influence of San Pablo Bay. Mount Veeder is an island of ancient seabed pushed up into a mountain surrounded by volcanic soils that typify the rest of Napa Valley. The rugged mountain terrain of extremely steep slopes above the fog renders shallow topsoil and minimal water retention, resulting in tiny berries with intense flavor and concentration. The Mount Veeder AVA is small, with only about 35 wineries producing 40,000 cases per vintage (about 1.3% of total Napa Valley production). Veeder is as good for Syrah as it is for Cabernet. It wafts from the glass with plush and vibrant dark fruits, black peppercorn, blueberry tones, plum jam and raspberries. articles.text: A series of six Asian cooking classes on Saturdays are being offered by Piedmont Adult School starting on October 29. The course is being taught by Chat Mingkwan, a native of Thailand who was trained in culinary arts in Rayon, France. Mingkwan began preparing Thai food as a child, working alongside his mother and aunt in their successful restaurant and hotel. He has traveled throughout Southeast Asia, studying local cuisines, and currently a cooking teacher, author, food and restaurant consultant. Students will receive instructions on the ingredients and techniques, and then break into small groups to prepare the recipes. The class then comes together to enjoy the meal they have created. The cost is $75 per class. Classes meet in the Student Center on the high school campus Instructor Chat Mingkwan was classically trained in cooking in Rayon, France. from 10:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. on Saturdays. Register online at Piedmontadultschool.org, or call the Adult School at 594-2655.

articles.text: Oakland Zoo recently helped rescue a dozen reptiles from TriState Zoological Park, a roadside attraction in Cumberland, Maryland. The Zoo was part of a fiveday rescue operation by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA), the group’s largest-ever rescue of animals from a roadside zoo. A total of 60 animals of 30 different species were recovered as a result of a legal settlement with Tri-State, formerly operated by Robert Candy. Members of the Oakland Zoo staff made the cross-country drive back to Oakland last weekend with the rescued reptiles. Oakland Zoo was among 14 accredited zoos and sanctuaries that assisted in the removal, transport, and immediate care of the animals rescued, which included reptiles, bears, exotic birds, and coatimundis. The facility had repeatedly failed to meet minimum federal standards for the care of animals established by the Animal Welfare Act (AWA). The animals were kept in small cages or enclosures and were left neglected, A Sulcata tortoise at the time Tri-State Zoological Park was shut down. Darren Minier, Director of Animal Welfare and Research at Oakland Zoo, helps rescue a tortoise from the roadside Tri-State Zoological Park in Cumberland, Maryland. PETA and Oakland Zoo staff outside of the now closed Tri-State Zoological Park.
articles.title: Oakland Zoo helps rescue reptiles in Maryland

articles.text: World-renowned conservationist and ethologist (the study of animal behavior) Jane Goodall made a rare appearance at the Oakland Zoo on October 6 for a private event with 350 guests. During her visit Goodall, currently a resident of England, spoke to 100 Oakland School District students and the Zoo’s Teen Wild Guides about her journey and stories of hope for animals, people, and the environment. Dr. Goodall last visited Oakland Zoo 15 years ago for the unveiling of a Gibbon habitat in the process of being built. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, October 19, 2022 your Oakland Zoo helps rescue reptiles in Maryland Oakland Zoo recently helped rescue a dozen reptiles from TriState Zoological Park, a roadside attraction in Cumberland, Maryland. The Zoo was part of a fiveday rescue operation by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA), the group’s largest-ever rescue of animals from a roadside zoo. A total of 60 animals of 30 different species were recovered as a result of a legal settlement with Tri-State, formerly operated by Robert Candy. Members of the Oakland Zoo staff made the cross-country drive back to Oakland last weekend with the rescued reptiles. Oakland Zoo was among 14 accredited zoos and sanctuaries that assisted in the removal, transport, and immediate care of the animals rescued, which included reptiles, bears, exotic birds, and coatimundis. The facility had repeatedly failed to meet minimum federal standards for the care of animals established by the Animal Welfare Act (AWA). The animals were kept in small cages or enclosures and were left neglected, A Sulcata tortoise at the time Tri-State Zoological Park was shut down. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers paused for a group photo last week at Hampton Park: Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Alicia Rivera, Melba Yee, Gloria DaSilva, Garrett Clifford, Priscilla Wanerus, Larry Olsen, Nancy Olsen, Mary Hedley, Martin Levy, Jim Kellogg, Mike Gallant, Jasmine Cai, Lisa Euphrat, Matt Gerhardt, Jim Kuo, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Jane Holland, Mark Davis, Brenda Ferrero, Kat Lang, Phil Witte, Christine Calliste, Helen Dong, Edith Lee, Stella Houston, Pat Keller, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Tally, Quincy Dong, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Elizabeth Richter, Noemi Alvarado, Laura Goldman with K-9 best friend Vivie, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome three first time walkers, Beth Cary, Mary Borrelli, and Jennifer Peltzen. Another strong turnout of 38 walkers and four K-9 best friends showed up on October 12 for a stroll to the edge of the city by the Walking on Wednesdays group. One area the group had not visited in some time was the Sandringham-Selborne-Estates loop near the top of Hampton Avenue. Additionally, they had not gotten to the uniquely named Wyngaard Avenue. The walkers went up Highland Avenue to Sheridan and Wildwood Avenues. On Sheridan there was a large persimmon tree in a front yard with a bounty of fruit, but not quite ripe. The trees that line Wildwood have some of the city’s best fall colors, and they seemed to be at their peak, as fallen leaves provided a burgundy sidewalk carpet. The walkers went up Crocker and onto Hampton Road Avenue, passing the always lovely Crocker Park (known as Bear Park to neighbors). The group reassembled at Hampton Park at the corner of LaSalle Avenue, where they posed for a group photo before embarking on the long trek to Wyngaard. The walkers ascended Hampton to Sandringham Road and then to the Marlborough Court cul-de-sac, where they were greeted by long-time walker Carol Long and her K-9 best friend Bailey. A half block later they explored Sandringham Place, another cul-de-sac. As an educational footnote, French speaking members of the group informed the others that cul-de-sac, means bottom of the sack. At the intersection of Sandringham and Selborne Drive, everyone enjoyed a wonderful view of the Bay. Going on Selborne the group made its way to Estates Drive and a short walk further brought them to the uniquely named Wyngaard Avenue. It is marked by columns of the original St. James Woods development, though the columns are nearly hidden behind wisteria vines. It was now time to answer the question: Who or what is Wyngaard? The closest to an answer was a search that revealed 86 percent of Wyngaards are found in South Africa which had a large Dutch population. But the connection to Piedmont remains unclear. Going down Wyngaard, the group viewed a home at the end of the street near Sandringham that is on the market for $3.5 million. They passed more beautiful homes, one of a Tudor half-timber of an Elizabethan architectural style, and another Storybook CHAPEL OF THE CHIMES - OAKLAND

articles.text: When you were expecting your first child you probably sought books to help you prepare for what was coming. Best sellers such as What to Expect When You’re Expecting, The Expectant Father, and Dr. Spock’s Baby and Child Care, helped inform millions of new parents about every aspect of pregnancy, birth, and childcare. Updated editions of these books are still on the market today – decades after their first publication. These days, you might be perusing the literature looking at what you can find about becoming a grandparent. Grandparenting books fall into a few general categories: Grandparent journals, personal memoirs, and how-to books for new grandparents. Grandparent journals/memory books are the top sellers on Amazon.com, and there are dozens of choices. Here are just a few: Grandmother’s/Grandfather’s Journal, by Blue Streak (#1 in Grandparenting Books), Tell Me Your Life Story, Grandma, by Questions About Me, Grandma’s Story, by Korie Herold. These books offer grandparents a simple and delightful way to share with a grandchild their personal details, life history, family lore, and other priceless treasures that can sometimes become lost over the years. It’s amazing how many things we don’t know about our grandparents simply because we never thought to ask them before they passed away. (Options for each book allow the grandparent to choose the journal with their correct grandparent name, i.e., Nana, Grandma, Papa, etc.) Personal memoirs seem to be trending for well-known celebrities and/or authors who would like to share the joys and challenges of becoming a grandparent. Many of these books have a humorous tone, such as Granny Diaries by Adair Lara. This is a brilliant and hilarious take on what to do (and not to do) when your millennial child becomes a first-time parent. Anna Quindlen is the author of Nanaville, Adventures in Grandparenting. Quindlen, who is known for her writing about her own experiences as a mother, now writes with humor and insight into her life as a Nana. Journalist Lesley Stahl wrote Becoming Grandma, The Joys and Science of the New Grandparenting. Along with sharing her personal experiences, Stahl interviews scientists and other famous grandparents on a broad range of relevant topics. All of these authors share their wisdom about how they managed to successfully shed the mantle of parent (to the young adults) and gracefully embrace their new Book ideas for grandparents. supportive role of grandparent/ wise elder. General grandparent books offer a broad range of topics to educate and inform new grandparents. The Modern Grandparent’s Handbook: The Ultimate Guide to the New Rules of Grandparenting, by Dr Georgia Witkin, was published ten years ago, but still offers great advice for today’s families. Unconditional Love, by Jane Isay, is a beautifully written book about the special connection between grandparents and grandchildren. It can help any senior in their journey to be a wise and loving grandparent. The Mindful Grandparent, The Art of Loving Our Children’s Children, by Marilyn McEntyre and Shirley Showalter may be the latest (published in May 2022) and greatest resource available for grandparents. These experienced authors provide spot-on advice for grandparents today and do so while always considering the best interests of all three generations in the family. The chapters are alternately written by each author, and each chapter ends with a brief recap of the key messages of the chapter for the reader. It is an exceptional contribution to the genre of grandparenting books. Whether you are expecting your first grandbaby or are trying to stay connected to a growing teenaged grandchild, these books will enhance your journey, warm your heart, and open your mind to your own special role of grandparent. As you read them, you are likely to gain insight into how to support your adult child in optimal ways, and you just may discover what legacy you want to leave for your grandchild. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn. com
articles.title: Essential reading for grandparents

articles.text: Homes are places of comfort and safety for the most part, but there are also inherent dangers in every home where risks do exist. As people age, the likelihood of falling and being seriously injured increases due to dizziness, medication side effects, or vision changes. An in-home care evaluation can be a solution by identifying problem areas and suggesting adaptations to minimize the chances of a slip or fall. Studies have found that someone who is living with dementia is at an increased risk for falling and being injured. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) charts falls among older adults and gives advice on how to intervene to prevent these accidents. According to the CDC, “falls among adults 65 and older caused 34,000 deaths in 2019, making it the leading cause of injury and death for that group.” Of the 1-in-4 older adults who fall each year, less than half tell their doctor, the CDC found. Still, 3 million seniors are treated in the ER for fall injuries and 1-in-5 reported falls lead to a broken bone or head injury. The CDC states that there are 800,000 patients hospitalized annually with a head injury or hip fracture. Room by Room The most dangerous room in a house isn’t even a room, it’s the stairs. According to Medical Guardian, a personal emergency response provider, a home with stairs has an added fall risk for seniors. The solution is ensuring there are adequate handrails on both sides of the stairs. These handrails should be secure; not wiggling when grabbed on to. The bathroom is considered the most dangerous room in the house for seniors, based on a CDC report which found that 235,000 people go to the ER each year after a fall in the bathroom and 14% of those are hospitalized. These injuries can happen while bathing or showering, but also when using the toilet. Grab bars can make a bathroom safer, as well as non-skid mats in the shower or tub, and removing any throw rugs. The kitchen has its own hazards, so falling isn’t the top concern in this room. Improper food storage and accidents while preparing food can lead to food poisoning and injuries like cuts or bruises, and possibly fires. Certainly, if someone is using a stepladder to reach a high shelf or liquids are spilled, there is a higher chance of a fall in this room. The living room and the bedroom can also have a high probability of falls, and for unexpected reasons: lighting and stability when standing. These are rooms where people tend to sit or lie down, but when people stand up, there can be sudden dizziness or stiffness in muscles and joints that contribute to falling down. Some solutions to make these rooms safer include remote controlled lighting, removing throw rugs, clearing clutter and cords that could be tripped over. Outside falls The challenges for older adults can also be found outside, so don’t forget about the garden, garage, and driveways. Gardening can be an excellent activity for elders who want a little exercise and time outdoors. But an inadvertently placed rake or shovel can lead to a trip and subsequent fall. Another consideration is the heat and physical exertion, which can leave someone lightheaded enough to fall. The key here is to remain hydrated, rest often, and keep tools safely stored when not in use. Outside walkways can be slippery, not just in winter, like after watering the lawn and plants. The risk for a traumatic brain injury is real with a fall on the driveway, according to Medical Guardian, so take steps to reduce the chance of a fall in this area. For example, install motion-sensor lights, use an assistive device when walking to the car or to get the mail, safely stow-away hoses, and keep pathways clear. Home care can address risks of falling A professionally trained caregiver knows how to look for fall risks in the home and what measures can be used to lessen the likelihood of a fall. Tasks like assistance with bathing or showering, post-surgery care, and dementia care can all be part of mitigating falls as a steady hand will help someone avoid a slip and fall. A complimentary in-home evaluation can help identify potential risks in each room of the house and include considerations for those who are living with memory impairment. Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. 5. One of the features I use the most, is attaching my signature to a PDF. This is done through the application Preview. To copy your signature onto a PDF: Open the Preview app then navigate to > Tools > Annotate > Signature > Manage signatures. You can either draw your signature on the trackpad with your finger, which I find very difficult, or take a picture of your signature written on a blank white piece of paper with a dark and thick pen. You can then save that signature. For example, I have my mother’s signature, for whom I am power of attorney, and my initials, and my full signature. This way, I can just basically paste it wherever I need it, whether it’s in a tax form or a contract. This signature is resizable. So, if it needs to be bigger, I just stretch the box that it is contained in, and I can move it anywhere in a PDF. 6. Keyboard shortcuts are another feature I depend on: I have made several. To customize your own, go to System Preferences > Keyboard > Text and click the + icon. You then decide the letter combination that you want, and then enter the text that will expand with this. For example, every time I write my address, I use the shortcut, “strt.” For my email address, cmm ,

articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear Macmama: My son was visiting, and he told me there were a lot of features I am not using on my iMac. For example, he said I could take a picture of my screen. Can you tell me how to do that? –Lissa, Oakland Dear Lissa: I wrote about some features in Monterey in March, but here are a few more including how to take a screenshot. 1. To take a picture, or screenshot of your whole screen, simultaneously press Command + Shift + 3. You will then see a small image of your screen appear in the lower left. If you click on that you can save it, share it via email or messages or even annotate it with text and symbols. To take a screenshot of a portion of your screen, press Command + Shift + 4. Then you will see a small target, and you can click and drag the portion you want to save. This is very useful for example, if you need to show your tech professional something that has popped up on your screen that is troublesome. 2. If a notif ication has appeared on your screen on the upper right, and then disappears, you can show it (and all notifications) again by simply clicking on the time and date on the upper right corner of your screen. 3. Spotlight is for more than just searching for files, you can do math equations. Another thing you can do is currency conversion. For example, if you’re going to Europe, you can type in €100, and it will show you the currency of your home country. 4. If you want to preview a file quickly, single click it, and press your spacebar. And to rename a file quickly and easily, highlight it by clicking it once, then click the Return key on your keyboard. When you’re finished, simply press the Return key again, and the new file name will be saved.

Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. Essential reading for grandparents THE MACMAMA By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear Macmama: My son was visiting, and he told me there were a lot of features I am not using on my iMac. For example, he said I could take a picture of my screen. Can you tell me how to do that? –Lissa, Oakland Dear Lissa: I wrote about some features in Monterey in March, but here are a few more including how to take a screenshot. 1. To take a picture, or screenshot of your whole screen, simultaneously press Command + Shift + 3. You will then see a small image of your screen appear in the lower left. If you click on that you can save it, share it via email or messages or even annotate it with text and symbols. To take a screenshot of a portion of your screen, press Command + Shift + 4. Then you will see a small target, and you can click and drag the portion you want to save. This is very useful for example, if you need to show your tech professional something that has popped up on your screen that is troublesome. 2. If a notif ication has appeared on your screen on the upper right, and then disappears, you can show it (and all notifications) again by simply clicking on the time and date on the upper right corner of your screen. 3. Spotlight is for more than just searching for files, you can do math equations. Another thing you can do is currency conversion. For example, if you’re going to Europe, you can type in €100, and it will show you the currency of your home country. 4. If you want to preview a file quickly, single click it, and press your spacebar. And to rename a file quickly and easily, highlight it by clicking it once, then click the Return key on your keyboard. When you’re finished, simply press the Return key again, and the new file name will be saved. 5. One of the features I use the most, is attaching my signature to a PDF. This is done through the application Preview. To copy your signature onto a PDF: Open the Preview app then navigate to > Tools > Annotate > Signature > Manage signatures. You can either draw your signature on the trackpad with your finger, which I find very difficult, or take a picture of your signature written on a blank white piece of paper with a dark and thick pen. You can then save that signature. For example, I have my mother’s signature, for whom I am power of attorney, and my initials, and my full signature. This way, I can just basically paste it wherever I need it, whether it’s in a tax form or a contract. This signature is resizable. So, if it needs to be bigger, I just stretch the box that it is contained in, and I can move it anywhere in a PDF. 6. Keyboard shortcuts are another feature I depend on: I have made several. To customize your own, go to System Preferences > Keyboard > Text and click the + icon. You then decide the letter combination that you want, and then enter the text that will expand with this. For example, every time I write my address, I use the shortcut, “strt.” For my email address, cmm , See MacMama on page 32 By Cynthia Kane When you were expecting your first child you probably sought books to help you prepare for what was coming. Best sellers such as What to Expect When You’re Expecting, The Expectant Father, and Dr. Spock’s Baby and Child Care, helped inform millions of new parents about every aspect of pregnancy, birth, and childcare. Updated editions of these books are still on the market today – decades after their first publication. These days, you might be perusing the literature looking at what you can find about becoming a grandparent. Grandparenting books fall into a few general categories: Grandparent journals, personal memoirs, and how-to books for new grandparents. Grandparent journals/memory books are the top sellers on Amazon.com, and there are dozens of choices. Here are just a few: Grandmother’s/Grandfather’s Journal, by Blue Streak (#1 in Grandparenting Books), Tell Me Your Life Story, Grandma, by Questions About Me, Grandma’s Story, by Korie Herold. These books offer grandparents a simple and delightful way to share with a grandchild their personal details, life history, family lore, and other priceless treasures that can sometimes become lost over the years. It’s amazing how many things we don’t know about our grandparents simply because we never thought to ask them before they passed away. (Options for each book allow the grandparent to choose the journal with their correct grandparent name, i.e., Nana, Grandma, Papa, etc.) Personal memoirs seem to be trending for well-known celebrities and/or authors who would like to share the joys and challenges of becoming a grandparent. Many of these books have a humorous tone, such as Granny Diaries by Adair Lara. This is a brilliant and hilarious take on what to do (and not to do) when your millennial child becomes a first-time parent. Anna Quindlen is the author of Nanaville, Adventures in Grandparenting. Quindlen, who is known for her writing about her own experiences as a mother, now writes with humor and insight into her life as a Nana. Journalist Lesley Stahl wrote Becoming Grandma, The Joys and Science of the New Grandparenting. Along with sharing her personal experiences, Stahl interviews scientists and other famous grandparents on a broad range of relevant topics. All of these authors share their wisdom about how they managed to successfully shed the mantle of parent (to the young adults) and gracefully embrace their new Book ideas for grandparents. supportive role of grandparent/ wise elder. General grandparent books offer a broad range of topics to educate and inform new grandparents. The Modern Grandparent’s Handbook: The Ultimate Guide to the New Rules of Grandparenting, by Dr Georgia Witkin, was published ten years ago, but still offers great advice for today’s families. Unconditional Love, by Jane Isay, is a beautifully written book about the special connection between grandparents and grandchildren. It can help any senior in their journey to be a wise and loving grandparent. The Mindful Grandparent, The Art of Loving Our Children’s Children, by Marilyn McEntyre and Shirley Showalter may be the latest (published in May 2022) and greatest resource available for grandparents. These experienced authors provide spot-on advice for grandparents today and do so while always considering the best interests of all three generations in the family. The chapters are alternately written by each author, and each chapter ends with a brief recap of the key messages of the chapter for the reader. It is an exceptional contribution to the genre of grandparenting books. Whether you are expecting your first grandbaby or are trying to stay connected to a growing teenaged grandchild, these books will enhance your journey, warm your heart, and open your mind to your own special role of grandparent. As you read them, you are likely to gain insight into how to support your adult child in optimal ways, and you just may discover what legacy you want to leave for your grandchild. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. articles.text: On a sunny day in August, 16 members of the Piedmont Seniors group visited Historic Ardenwood Farm in Fremont, where they got a glimpse into life on a family farm that was active between 1890 and 1930. Ardenwood was named after a forest area described in Shakespeare’s play As you Like It. Since 1985 this fully functioning farm has been operated by the East Bay Regional Park District. The best way to get one’s bearings is to hop aboard a train that encircles the 205-acre farm. As the train made its journey, the Seniors saw cattle grazing in the pastures, goats, chickens, and eucalyptus groves which surround the property. There is a Deer Park Station, where you can disembark and explore the farm by foot and even have a picnic. After the train ride, the group took a short walk to the Patterson House, home to three generations of the Patterson family. Completed in 1857, the house was later expanded with a Queen Ann addition in 1889. The Seniors explored the remnants of the once vast estate of George and Clara Patterson, whose family farmed the land for over 100 years, beginning in the 1850s. As transportation options were limited throughout the countryside in the 19th century, railroads served as an important way to connect many of the farms in the East Bay. One of the highlights of the day was the tour of the Patterson House, led by a costumed docent in period attire of the time. The docents were eager to explain the social graces of the Victorian era and demonstrate some of the useful gadgets frequently used in this time frame. An interesting gadget Piedmont Seniors with a docent in front of the 100-year old Patterson House. All Aboard. The Piedmont Seniors group in front of the Ardenwood train station before boarding a train for a trip around the farm. Pictured are: (front) Nancy Hinsch, Janet Epstein, Sandra Curach, Mona Jamieson, Madeline Hall, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, and Yorkman Lowe; (back): Penny Robb, Gregory Jurin, Carole Jones, Cheryl Stanton, Irene Westler, and Robert Hall. Not pictured: Jim Ayotle and Rick Luciano. was a bed warmer, consisting of a metal container shaped like a modern frying pan which would be filled with embers and placed under the covers of the bed. The tour was a glimpse into life on a working farm in the mid- 19th century. It is particularly informative for groups of elementary school students who visit, so they can visualize what life must have been like during this period. Students occasionally allowed to assist in the processing of crops including corn, wheat and hay. Other attractions on the farm include a blacksmith shop with an actual blacksmith on duty, a greenhouse, gazebo, a walnut orchard, a milk house and a myriad of farm animals. You can also order food from a café on weekends and enjoy a pleasant picnic lunch on the spacious grounds. During their visit to Ardenwood, the seniors worked up a hearty appetite, so they ventured to Buon Hayward in Hayward Appetito for a delicious lunch. One of the members even provided the group with a special treat of home-made French bread, It was a delightful outing for a group of lucky Seniors. I encourage all residents to participate in these important events. 2. Costly upgrades to City Center? Public safety and emergency preparation have been and always will be a priority for Piedmont. In 2019, the city staff began an assessment process to determine the scope (renovation vs. replacement) of improvements that would be necessary to bring our aging public safety buildings up to current standards. Since then, Piedmont was fortunate to receive $2.6 million from the Federal American Rescue Plan, which Council immediately allocated for the renovation of the 911 Dispatch Center. With our city budget almost entirely dependent upon property taxes, identifying funding sources for large infrastructure projects will remain a significant challenge. Council will continue to evaluate the costs and benefits of different financing approaches in this rising interest rate environment. If our community decides to invest in further upgrades to the civic center, I am confident that talented architects will be able to retain the charming exterior aesthetic of City Hall. 2. Costly upgrades to City Center? Funding deferred maintenance is a challenge most cities face. We will need to carefully study our current infrastructure to determine what is needed. These upgrades are needed to modernize and maintain the core essential services that we all value. Finding funding sources to allow improvements to occur in a cost-effective way must be a top priority for our City. Piedmont is known for its beautiful homes and architecture. Many of us chose to move here because of our city’s size, treelined streets, and charming city center. Preserving the architectural aesthetic of our current civic center is essential to any renovations we undertake. JENNIFER LONG Incumbent 1. Campaign Strategy I am focused on connecting with voters in person. Outreach is critical to campaigning, as well as to the work of Council. It allows for diverse voices to be part of solutions. During a campaign, voters have the opportunity to hear from candidates, and hopefully learn more about them and how they might approach issues and problem solve. I have enjoyed meeting residents and hearing about their concerns. I plan to incorporate what I have heard into my decision making on issues that impact our community. Sudoku Solution SUDOKU SOLUTION BRIDGET HARRIS 1. Campaign Strategy I will focus my energy and resources on further educating the residents on their right to vote on a re-zone of park and municipal properties. The residents of Piedmont have the right to decide what areas of Piedmont will be rezoned to accommodate multi-family units. Section 17.08 of the Code of the City of Piedmont provides if a use is not permitted in a zone it is not allowed. Zone B includes park and public lands. Pursuant to Section 17.22.020 of the Code, multi-family units are not allowed in Zone B. A reclassification of a zone requires a majority vote; therefore, I will continue advocating the requirement of a vote. This is simply a vote on options. As mentioned in Question 2, there are safety improvements needed for certain city structures. I will also focus my energies on what is necessary to improve our public safety facilities. 2. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, October 19, 2022 Pool Bids Continued from page 1 ipated costs, the council voted to reopen bidding and expand bidding eligibility to a wider range of contractors, while retaining the current design. The two contractors who submitted bids were SJ Amoroso at $24,597,000 and Lathrop Construction at $26,149,000. The city engineer’s cost estimate is $21.6 million. “We are disappointed but not deterred,” said City Administrator Sara Lillevand. “By casting a wider net for contractors, I am optimistic that we will find a firm to complete the project within the City’s available resources.” “I think the key thing about this process we are in right now is we need the competition,” said Clarence Mamuyac, President of ELS. “Generally, when we put these types of projects out to bid, we are looking for four or five bidders.” Mamuyac advised against making changes to the design, specifically the electrification of the pool, since so much community effort and staff time has been dedicated to full electrification. He also discouraged the idea of waiting for costs to go down, citing that rarely occurs. Coupled with inflation, steep rises in construction costs have been driven by supply and demand issues and labor shortages beginning in many areas during the first year of Covid and its general disruption to businesses worldwide. According to a press release by the city on October 14, “between July 2020 and July 2022, the California Construction Cost Index increased by 30%. In comparison, the 10-year average annual increase between 2010 and 2020 was 2.4%. The 20-year average annual increase was 2.9%.” New bids are due within 30 days and the city plans to process them by Thanksgiving, November, 24. Lillevand said it may be possible to award a contract at the December City Council meeting. “The thing we got the most right was the timing of the issuing of the bonds,” said Lillevand, explaining that the city saved an estimated $5 million by issuing bonds in 2020 as opposed to issuing them now. The new community pool as designed will include a 27-meter competition pool with diving wells, a 3,177 square foot activity pool with three 25-yard lap lanes, and a one-story building with locker rooms, two gender neutral changing rooms, and a rooftop pavilion.
